question: You add a required column with AddField(default='TBD'). Django's generated SQL adds the column with a database default and then immediately drops that default. Why does this break a rolling deploy?
choices: Old code still running during the rollout inserts rows without naming the column; with the DB default gone, the NOT NULL column rejects those inserts — db_default persists the default and fixes it
The DROP DEFAULT statement takes an exclusive table lock that blocks all reads for the duration of the rollout window
New code reads the Python-side default while the database returns NULL, so the two code versions silently diverge on the value
The migration becomes irreversible once the default is dropped, so a failed deploy strands the schema mid-change
explanation: A rolling deploy has a coexistence window where old and new code hit the same schema, and the old code's INSERT statements simply don't mention the new column — only a database-level default can fill it in. Django drops the DB default because it manages defaults in Python at the ORM layer, which is safe on a single-version system but exactly wrong mid-rollout. db_default (Django 5.0+) persists the default in the schema itself, so the DROP DEFAULT never happens and old-code inserts keep succeeding. Lock contention is a real but separate migration concern, and the failure here is rejected writes, not divergent reads or irreversibility.

question: You delete legacy_ref — a NOT NULL column with no default — from the model, and the RemoveField migration is correctly staged post-deploy. Yet during the rollout, as soon as new-code servers come up, their INSERTs start failing. Why?
choices: RemoveField acquires an exclusive table lock that blocks concurrent inserts for the duration of the rollout window
Django's runtime model state diverges from the schema, so the ORM raises as soon as it encounters a column it no longer knows about

The new code's INSERTs no longer name legacy_ref, but the column still exists until the post-deploy drop — NOT NULL with no default rejects those writes; a pre-deploy step must first make the column nullable or give it a db_default
The staging is inverted: destructive operations must run pre-deploy so that both code versions see the same schema throughout the rollout
explanation: The remove side of the coexistence window is symmetric to the add side: the moment the field leaves the model, Django stops listing it in INSERT statements — and the column is deliberately still in the schema, because the drop is staged after the old code is gone. A NOT NULL column with no default rejects any insert that doesn't name it, so the new code breaks against a column only the old code still fills. Field removal is therefore inherently two-phase: a pre-deploy AlterField making the column nullable (or persisting a db_default), then the post-deploy RemoveField — django-syzygy generates that pre-deploy half automatically; with django-safemigrate you stage it yourself. No lock is involved since the drop hasn't run yet; the ORM never introspects the schema at runtime; and moving destructive drops pre-deploy would break the old code instead — the mirror-image failure.

question: One release both adds Order.tracking_number (a nullable column the new code reads and writes) and deletes Order.legacy_ref — a nullable column the currently-deployed code still reads, which the new code drops entirely. The developer makes both model edits, runs makemigrations once, and gets a single migration containing the AddField and the RemoveField. The pipeline uses django-safemigrate, so a single Safe label must now cover the whole file. What does the three-stage model say about this migration?
choices: It fits no slot, and no label can fix that. A migration's stage is a property of its operations, and this file mixes an additive one — AddField, pre-deploy by nature, harmless to old code — with a destructive one — RemoveField, post-deploy by nature, safe only once old code is gone. Label the file Safe.before_deploy() and the drop runs while still-deployed old code SELECTs legacy_ref: crash during rollout. Label it Safe.after_deploy() and the new code spends the rollout reading tracking_number before the column exists. The fix is upstream of labelling: split the model edits so each makemigrations run emits a single-stage migration — the AddField marked before_deploy, the RemoveField after_deploy. This is exactly the ambiguity syzygy's guardrail exists to catch: it raises a system check error on migrations mixing inferred stages, refusing to guess

Mark it Safe.after_deploy(): when operations conflict, the destructive one sets the safety bar, so the whole file inherits the later slot — the AddField merely waits a little longer, which additive operations tolerate by definition
Mark it Safe.before_deploy(): legacy_ref is already nullable, and nullable columns are safe to drop at any time — nothing at the database level can reject a write over a column that accepts NULL

Keep one file but mark it Safe.after_deploy(delay=timedelta(days=7)): the delay guarantees every old-code server has drained before the migration applies, which makes the combined file safe in both directions
explanation: The three-stage model's premise is that every migration sits on one side of the code swap, and the stage is determined by what its operations do to the coexistence window: additive changes leave old code's world intact (pre-deploy), destructive changes remove something old code may still touch (post-deploy). A file containing both is therefore not mislabelled but unlabelable — the two operations need to run on opposite sides of the same rollout, and a label applies to the file as a unit. Working both labels through the window proves it: before_deploy drops legacy_ref while the old version's SELECTs still name the column — every such query errors for the duration of the rollout; after_deploy withholds tracking_number while the new version's queries already reference it — same failure, other column, other direction. The guidance names this exact situation: a migration that fits none of the slots usually means several model edits were bundled into one run, and the cure is to split the edits so each generated file is single-stage. syzygy encodes the same rule as tooling — mixed inferred stages fail its system check, forcing an explicit decision. The distractors each generalize a half-truth: 'most conservative label wins' assumes waiting is free, but an additive migration the new code depends on is not optional during rollout — deferring it converts safety into breakage; 'nullable is droppable' confuses the two directions of the removal problem — nullability protects inserts from the new code, but the running old code still reads the column by name, and no DEFAULT or NULL saves a SELECT against a dropped column; and delay= only postpones when safemigrate applies an after_deploy migration — it stretches the wait, but the AddField trapped in the same file is still late by construction, so the rollout window is broken regardless of the timer's length.
